'It's common for there to be speculation and headlines:' Unity exec addresses acquisition rumors
Unity senior vice president of product Adam Smith says speculation over M&A tends to follow strong quarterly results.
Bryant Francis
,
Senior Editor
,
GameDeveloper.com
November 16, 2026
schedule
4 Min Read
Logo via Unity, illustration by Morena via Adobe Stock.
Developers, industry professionals, and Wall Street investors have all had reason to keep an eye on Unity lately. Earlier this month, Reuters reported that the company was "in talks" with the investment group that had recently
acquired Electronic Arts
—the one led by Silver Lake and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF)—to potentially go private in a full buyout. Now a Unity executive is weighing in on Reuters' story, saying that "it is extraordinarily common for there to be speculation and headlines" after a company like Unity posts strong quarterly results, and there's "nothing else to say" about said conversations.
That sentiment comes from Unity senior vice president of product Adam Smith, who commented on the rumor in an exclusive interview with GameDeveloper.com about
Unity's new fellowship program
aimed at supporting a select group of developers in their pre-launch push. "That's a common type of thing that happens when you have the type of quarter that we just had, with the type of forward look we provided," he remarked, adding that his immediate concern was heading to
Unite Tokyo
to spend time with the Unity development community.
Related:
Paradox Interactive names new CEO
It was indeed a strong quarter for Unity, which reported a 32 percent increase in revenue year over year in its recent presentation, an increase from about $470.6 million to $622 million. Unity still lost $121.6 million, but that's a 4 percent improvement on last year's loss of $126.8 million. Once again the company's advertising division, Grow Solutions, the company's advertising division, drove those gains with a 43 percent increase in revenue, jumping from $318 million to $457 million. But Create Solutions, which houses the game development engine, also saw a robust 8 percent increase in growth, going from $152 million to $165 million.
And that forward-looking guidance Smith mentioned? It states that Unity experts to earn $683 million in Q4 2026, up 65-67 percent from last year. It's some much-needed positive prognostication for a company that spent two years laying off
thousands of employees
following the decision to reverse a
massively unpopular Runtime Fee policy
that led to the exit of major executives like
CEO John Riccitiello
.
The company's new CEO, Matthew Bromberg, has promised its customers "
stability
" as the company gets back on its feet—and said stability may indeed be reflected in said financial results. But news of a possible buyout may have given some Unity users a shiver down their spine, as the prospective purchasing partner had already proven to be a destabilizing force in the game industry.
Related:
Unity's new fellowship program offers cash and dedicated support for indie devs
Unity's financial results apparently attracted controversial prospective buyers
Those not clued in to the complicated (often
calamitous
) world of game industry mergers & acquisitions in the last few years may be surprised to hear of developer concern over a possible buyout of Unity. But it's not just the prospect of a buyout—it's who would be doing the buying. The investment group that reportedly approached Unity was one led by the Saudi PIF and Silver Lake Partners, the same group that recently acquired Battlefield, The Sims, and
Apex Legends
developer Electronic Arts. The PIF already owns an eight percent stake in Unity.
In the wake of said acquisition, EA
laid off 400 employees
and shut down some of its celebrated studios, including Mass Effect and Dragon Age developer BioWare. Before those layoffs took place, employees shared concerns about the state of EA
in comments made to GameDeveloper.com
, many of which mirror worries being shared online by other professionals. Those concerns included uncertainty over the company’s future and concern that their new parent organization's
political ties to the government of Saudi Arabia
may impact their work.
Related:
Newly-proposed EU law could place tight restrictions on free-to-play games
The possibility of similar events occurring at Unity may not sit well with those hoping for the stability previously promised by Bromberg.
According to Smith—himself a former Unity customer who recalled using the software when it was an Apple-only application—the company is aware of its users' desire for a stable and reliable business partner, and its recent positive financial results reflect its ability to meet those needs. "We're very proud of of the work we've done, because we cannot reporter quarters like that if we are not enabling our developers to succeed by creating the best player experience for most of the world's population," he said.
"About 3 billion players play Made With Unity content on a monthly basis, and we had a lot of work to do to rebuild ourselves in that way. I think we've done that, and we still have a long ways to ago. But our developers are succeeding, and that's the only reason we're able to report the type of output we were able to last week."
